thread.title: Berkshire Hathaway: Intrinsic Value Estimates Exceed $240 Per Class B Share - Berkshire Hathaway, Inc. Cl A (NYSE:BRK.A)

author: Left Shark Investing
title: Berkshire Hathaway: Intrinsic Value Estimates Exceed $240 Per Class B Share - Berkshire Hathaway, Inc. Cl A (NYSE:BRK.A)
text:
In early 2017, I wrote an article on Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE: BRK.A ) (NYSE: BRK.B ) intrinsic value. At the time, I asserted Berkshire was worth $200-215 per share - a valuation range briefly exceeded earlier this year. Several readers asked me to update my analysis to account for changes that have occurred in the interim. Given appreciation of and additions to Berkshire's investment portfolio, higher cash balances, and higher pre-tax earnings coupled with a lower tax rate, I now derive a value modestly in excess of $240 per Class B share or ~24% upside at today's price. Importantly, based on my (very) preliminary estimate of Q2 book value, there would be approximately 10% downside to the share repurchase authorization.
I estimate that Berkshire's operating businesses will generate $19.5 billion in after-tax earnings this year. To calculate this number, I assume non-GEICO insurance businesses break even on an underwriting basis, burden the operating businesses with hold co. interest expense, asset-level amortization, and include estimated equity method earnings, excluding KHC. To this, I apply a 16x multiple for a total value of the operating businesses of $311 billion. Below is a summary calculation of my 2018 estimates:
Operating businesses 2018 Est. Earnings BNSF 5,511 BHE 2,632 Manufacturing, Service & Retail 8,447 Financial Services 1,684 GEICO 945 Equity method (excluding KHC) 544 Hold co. interest (300) Total 19,463 Multiple 16 Value 311,406
It is notable that many of Berkshire's operating businesses have materially increased earnings before any consideration of tax code changes. For instance, pre-tax profits at BNSF were up 12.5% y/y. Year-to-date, total carloads and intermodal are up 5.1% - well in excess of the industry average. In their manufacturing segment, pre-tax earnings are up 25% or 11% after accounting for a charge taken in the 1st quarter of 2017. Even before accounting for positive reserve development, earnings were up strongly at GEICO. I believe it is safe to say that Berkshire's operating businesses are benefiting from significant investments over the preceding years, capable management teams, and a generally supportive economic environment. For this reason, I do not think that a 16x multiple is aggressive when considering operational performance, the peer multiples of Berkshire's major operating subsidiaries, and the prevailing economic and interest rate conditions.
Turning to the investment portfolio, using Berkshire's most recent 13-F filing and current (5/23) market prices, the equity portfolio, including KHC, has a fair market value of ~$199 billion. To this, I add $20 billion in bonds and $89 billion of cash & t-bills (total cash less $20 billion withholding). From this, I net my estimate of the present value of Berkshire's deferred tax liability at $26 billion versus a stated value of $56 billion (10 years at an 8% discount rate). This discount represents the fact that Berkshire's cash obligation to pay these taxes is likely to occur over a very long period.
Investments Equities (5/23/18) 199,516 Excess cash 88,562 Fixed maturities 19,920 PV of DTL (26,000) Net value of investments 281,998
Adding the value of the operating businesses ($311 billion) to the net value of the investment portfolio ($282 billion) results in a total valuation of $593 billion or $241 per share.
Another way to calculate Berkshire's valuation is so-called look-thru earnings or consolidating Berkshire's proportional share of earnings in equity investees as if they owned the entire business. In this exercise, operating earnings are accounted for in the same manner as the sum-of-the-parts methodology. Regarding the investment portfolio, using consensus estimates for Berkshire's equity investees, I get $13.6 billion in proportional earnings. Note this number is higher than Berkshire's stated investment income because it includes both dividends and retained earnings - as if Berkshire owned the entire business. I assume a 4% yield on the bond portfolio for total investment earnings of $14.4 billion or $12.2 billion net of tax at a 15% rate. Berkshire's investment income tax rate is lower than its overall corporate rate given the dividend received deduction. Note, Berkshire holds tens of billions of t-bills, however, since we calculate the value of these bills as a proxy for cash, adding the investment income generated by them would be double counting.
Operating businesses 2018 Est. Earnings Total 19,463 Investments Equity 13,610 Bonds 797 Total 14,407 Taxes (2,161) Proportional income from investments 12,246 Total 31,709 Multiple 16 Value of earnings 507,341 Excess cash 88,562 Total value 595,903 Per share $ 241.65
Price-to-book is not a particularly rigorous valuation exercise because it does not give any indication of the productivity of the equity in the business. Over the past 30 years, Berkshire's price-to-book ratio averaged 1.59x. At the current price of $195, Berkshire trades at 1.34x my estimate of Q2 book. Readers should note that Berkshire is likely to see a sharp increase in book value during Q2 given appreciation of the investment portfolio, nearly $5 billion in AAPL alone and operating earnings. Meanwhile, both my sum-of-the-parts and look-thru earnings estimate imply a price-to-book of 1.66x. However, this does not suggest that if Berkshire traded at my estimate of intrinsic value, it would necessarily be more expensive than in the past. To the contrary, a lower tax rate has created a step-function increase in return on equity. For example, BNSF's earnings increased 37% in the 1st quarter, in large part due to a lower tax rate while equity invested in that business only increased 18% (almost all the result of a write-down of deferred tax liabilities). Holding all else constant, the higher a company's return on equity, the greater its market capitalization should be relative to that equity. As Berkshire's operating businesses now produce higher returns on equity, Berkshire's price-to-book multiple should increase as well. For this reason, I do not believe 1.66x book value is a particularly heroic assumption given it can be justified by both earnings and sum-of-the-parts methodologies.
Given the recent rise in interest rates, I think it is appropriate to point out that Berkshire is positioned to outperform in a higher interest rate regime. First, Berkshire has massive equity investments in interest rate sensitive financials. The cumulative investment in WFC, BAC, USB, BK, and MTB is $58 billion. Second, Berkshire's cash position is the ultimate short duration asset that can be used to purchase increasing amounts of earnings the higher rates go. Third, Berkshire predominately competes for deals with private equity or corporations that use debt or highly valued equity to make acquisitions. For this reason, if higher rates entail higher financing costs and lower equity valuations, Berkshire should become more competitive. An offset to this will be Berkshire's economically sensitive businesses, increased cost of debt at some operating companies, and lower values for some of the equity holdings. While it is difficult to tell whether Berkshire is a net beneficiary of higher rates, I believe it can be said that the negatives will be far less at Berkshire than most other companies.
Finally, while it is fun to talk about theoretical, even if well-grounded price targets, it is perhaps more important to think about downside protection. My current estimate of Q2 book value at $359 billion implies Berkshire's repurchase authorization would be $175 share or 10% below the current price. I am not suggesting that the price cannot go below this level or that book value cannot decline, however, it is notable that the share has not breached the 1.2x level since the authorization was introduced.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BRK.B.
